title: Math library functions and math.h
learningObjectives: Explain the concept and its C language rules.
Trace the example and explain data flow.
Identify common errors and boundary conditions.
Apply the concept in a small tested program.

understand.concept: The math.h header declares mathematical functions such as sqrt, pow, sin, cos, floor and ceil. Functions commonly operate on double values; domain errors, range errors, floating-point precision and implementation behaviour must be considered.
understand.whyItMatters: Using the standard math library avoids reimplementing common numerical operations, but callers must still validate inputs and interpret floating-point results appropriately.
understand.analogy: Treat a function or pointer operation as an explicit contract between caller and callee.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's formal rules for types, object lifetime, scope and linkage.

explain.narrative:
The math.h header declares mathematical functions such as sqrt, pow, sin, cos, floor and ceil. Functions commonly operate on double values; domain errors, range errors, floating-point precision and implementation behaviour must be considered.

When applying this concept, check declared types, preconditions, object lifetime and all control-flow paths. Compile with warnings enabled and test both typical and boundary inputs.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: sqrt returns the square root as a double. The format %.2f prints two digits after the decimal point. Some toolchains require linking the math library explicitly, for example with a compiler-specific -lm option.

practise.guidedTask: Predict the result and explain why the literal is written as 81.0.
practise.independentTask: Calculate the hypotenuse using sqrt and pow or multiplication. Validate inputs and compare floating-point values with a tolerance when appropriate.
hints: Include math.h for declarations rather than inventing your own prototype.
Floating-point equality can be unsuitable for results affected by rounding.
Compiler and linker command-line options differ by platform.
